vignette:
She is 42, an African woman who has spent most of her adult life working on trains. Even now, she speaks about railways with the kind of practical affection that comes from years of repetition: the weight of the radio in her hand, the rhythm of checking doors, the responsibility of moving strangers safely from one place to another. Before everything happened, she says she liked the order of the job. Trains ran on schedules. Signals meant something. If she stayed alert and did her work well, people arrived where they were meant to go.

The thing that changed her life happened several years ago, when she was living in her home country during a period of political unrest. She does not tell it all at once. Over several conversations, she gives pieces of it, then falls silent, watching my face carefully. She had been stopped on her way home and accused of helping people seen as disloyal to the authorities. She remembers the room first: no windows, a metal chair, the smell of sweat and damp concrete. Then she remembers hands on her shoulders, the sound of men laughing, and the confusion of trying to explain herself while already knowing explanations would not matter. She was held for days. She was beaten, deprived of sleep, threatened, and humiliated. She says the worst part was not only the pain but the deliberate way it was done, as if the point was to teach her that she had no control over her own body or fate. At one point she became convinced she would die there and that no one would know what had happened to her.

When she was eventually released, she returned home physically injured and strangely detached. Her husband tells her later that she moved through the house like a visitor. At the time, she is mostly focused on surviving the next hour. Loud voices make her whole body tense. If someone comes up behind her, she flinches hard enough to drop what she is holding. At night she does not sleep properly. She drifts off, then wakes soaked in sweat, heart pounding, sometimes already on her feet before she fully knows where she is. In the dreams she is back in the cell, unable to brace herself because she cannot predict what is coming next. Some mornings she sits on the edge of the bed and avoids looking at her husband because she cannot bear to see pity or fear in his face.

Later, after she and her husband relocate and she returns to railway work, she hopes routine will repair something in her. In some ways, the structure helps. She learns new routes, new procedures, a new uniform. She becomes known as competent and steady. Passengers see a conductor who is firm, efficient, and polite. Her colleagues know she is reliable. What they do not see is how carefully she manages herself to get through a shift. She scans each platform automatically, not just for safety hazards but for men standing too close, voices that sound aggressive, doors that might shut her into a small space. If she has to walk through a narrow carriage crowded with passengers, she feels her breathing change. If someone argues or refuses instructions, she experiences a flash of heat and panic that feels much larger than the moment. She can usually keep her face composed until she reaches the staff compartment, where she grips the counter and waits for the shaking in her hands to pass.

At home, her world has grown smaller than she wants to admit. She loves her husband and says he has been patient, but she often keeps parts of herself sealed off from him. When he asks what is wrong after a bad night, she says she is just tired. She avoids news from her home country because even brief footage of uniforms, detention centers, or shouting crowds can stay with her for days. She no longer likes being touched unexpectedly, even by people she trusts. Family gatherings exhaust her. She positions herself near exits in restaurants and on trains when she is not working. She checks locks more than once before bed, then lies awake listening for sounds that do not belong.

What troubles her almost as much as fear is the way the past intrudes into ordinary moments. A passenger banging on a locked door can suddenly become the sound of fists on metal. The fluorescent buzz in a station office can pull her back to that room before she has time to remind herself where she is. Sometimes she loses pieces of conversations because she has drifted into a memory without meaning to. She becomes irritated with herself afterward. She says she used to be warm and easy with people, and now she feels watchful, as if some part of her is always on duty.

She is ashamed of how often she blames herself, despite knowing intellectually that she was powerless. She wonders whether she should have said less, said more, fought harder, stayed quieter. The questions loop most when she is alone. Still, she keeps going to work. She irons her uniform, checks her schedule, and steps onto the train. She says the passengers do not know that every day she is performing two jobs at once: conducting the train, and persuading her body that this journey is not the one she took years ago when she was carried somewhere against her will.
